title: Probability
seo_title: Grade 7 Probability Worksheets: Likelihood, Theoretical and Experimental Probability
standard_text: Understand that the probability of a chance event is a number between 0 and 1 that expresses the likelihood of the event occurring. Approximate the probability of a chance event by collecting data and observing its long-run relative frequency, and predict the approximate relative frequency given the probability. Develop a probability model and use it to find probabilities of events.
meta_desc: Free Grade 7 probability worksheets: likelihood from 0 to 1, theoretical probability with spinners, marbles and number cubes, the complement, experimental probability and predictions. 100 practice questions with an answer key.
key_big: P(event) = favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes, a number from 0 to 1.
key_sub: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). To predict, multiply the probability by the number of tries.
body_html:
What probability means

A probability is a number from 0 to 1 that tells how likely an event is.

ProbabilityMeaning
0impossible
less than 1/2unlikely
1/2equally likely
more than 1/2likely
1certain

Theoretical probability

When all outcomes are equally likely: P(event) = number of favorable outcomes ÷ total number of outcomes. The complement is the event not happening: P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

Experimental probability

Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ number of tries. To predict, multiply the probability by the number of tries. More tries usually bring the experimental probability closer to the theoretical one.

Example

A bag has 3 red and 5 blue marbles. Find P(red) and P(not red).

P(red) = 3 ÷ (3 + 5) = 3/8.

P(not red) = 1 − 3/8 = 5/8.

Answer: 3/8 and 5/8

Example

P(rolling a 5) = 1/6. About how many 5s in 120 rolls?

1/6 × 120 = 20.

Answer: about 20

Common mistakes

  • Comparing to the other outcomes: 3 red and 5 blue gives 3/8, not 3/5.
  • Forgetting the complement: P(not red) is 1 − P(red).
  • Expecting an experiment to match exactly: results vary, especially with few tries.

faq.q: How do you find a probability?
faq.a: Divide the number of favorable outcomes by the total number of equally likely outcomes. A bag with 3 red and 5 blue marbles has P(red) = 3/8.

faq.q: What is the complement of an event?
faq.a: It is the event not happening. The two probabilities add to 1, so P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

faq.q: What is the difference between experimental and theoretical probability?
faq.a: Theoretical probability comes from the possible outcomes. Experimental probability comes from what actually happened in trials, such as 28 heads in 50 flips = 28/50.

faq.q: How do I make a prediction?
faq.a: Multiply the probability by the number of trials. If P(5) = 1/6, expect about 1/6 × 120 = 20 fives in 120 rolls.

items.q: Which probability best describes an event that is impossible?
items.e: Probability goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). 1/2 means equally likely. Near 0 is unlikely and near 1 is likely.

items.q: Which probability best describes an event that is certain?
items.e: Probability goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). 1/2 means equally likely. Near 0 is unlikely and near 1 is likely.

items.q: Which probability best describes an event that is equally likely as not?
items.e: Probability goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). 1/2 means equally likely. Near 0 is unlikely and near 1 is likely.

items.q: Which probability best describes an event that is unlikely?
items.e: Probability goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). 1/2 means equally likely. Near 0 is unlikely and near 1 is likely.

items.q: Which probability best describes an event that is likely?
items.e: Probability goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). 1/2 means equally likely. Near 0 is unlikely and near 1 is likely.

items.q: How likely is rolling a 7 on a standard number cube (1 to 6)?
items.e: It can never happen, so the probability is 0.

items.q: How likely is the sun rising tomorrow morning?
items.e: It will surely happen, so the probability is 1.

items.q: How likely is a fair coin landing on heads?
items.e: Half of the outcomes work, so the probability is 1/2.

items.q: How likely is rolling a 1 on a number cube?
items.e: Only 1 of 6 outcomes works. 1/6 is close to 0.

items.q: How likely is rolling a number less than 6 on a number cube?
items.e: 5 of 6 outcomes work. 5/6 is close to 1.

items.q: How likely is picking a red card from a deck with 26 red and 26 black cards?
items.e: Half of the outcomes work, so the probability is 1/2.

items.q: How likely is picking a blue marble from a bag of only red marbles?
items.e: It can never happen, so the probability is 0.

items.q: An event has a probability of 0.95. How would you describe it?
items.e: 0.95 is close to 1, so the event is likely.

items.q: An event has a probability of 0.08. How would you describe it?
items.e: 0.08 is close to 0, so the event is unlikely.

items.q: An event has a probability of 0.5. How would you describe it?
items.e: 0.5 is exactly 1/2, so the event is equally likely as not.

items.q: An event has a probability of 1.2. How would you describe it?
items.e: A probability is never less than 0 or more than 1.

items.q: Which number cannot be a probability?
items.e: A probability is between 0 and 1. A negative number cannot be a probability.

items.q: Which event is more likely?
items.e: The closer to 1, the more likely. 0.7 is the largest.

items.q: Which is the same probability as 3/4?
Which is the same probability as 40%?
The spinner has equal sections. What is the probability of landing on red?
items.e: 2 of the 4 equal sections are red, so P(red) = 2/4 = 1/2.

items.q: The spinner has equal sections. What is the probability of landing on blue?
items.e: 3 of the 6 equal sections are blue, so P(blue) = 3/6 = 1/2.

items.q: The spinner has equal sections. What is the probability of landing on red?
items.e: 4 of the 8 equal sections are red, so P(red) = 4/8 = 1/2.

items.q: The spinner has equal sections. What is the probability of landing on yellow?
items.e: 1 of the 5 equal sections are yellow, so P(yellow) = 1/5. Not 1/4: divide by all 5 sections, not just the sections that are not yellow.

items.q: The spinner has equal sections. What is the probability of landing on blue?
items.e: 2 of the 6 equal sections are blue, so P(blue) = 2/6 = 1/3. Not 1/2: divide by all 6 sections, not just the sections that are not blue.

items.q: The spinner has equal sections. What is the probability of landing on green?
items.e: 3 of the 8 equal sections are green, so P(green) = 3/8. Not 3/5: divide by all 8 sections, not just the sections that are not green.

items.q: You pick one marble without looking. What is the probability it is red?
items.e: There are 3 red marbles out of 8 in all. P(red) = 3/8.

items.q: You pick one marble without looking. What is the probability it is green?
items.e: There are 4 green marbles out of 12 in all. P(green) = 4/12 = 1/3.

items.q: You pick one marble without looking. What is the probability it is green?
items.e: There are 6 green marbles out of 10 in all. P(green) = 6/10 = 3/5.

items.q: You pick one marble without looking. What is the probability it is yellow?
items.e: There are 3 yellow marbles out of 10 in all. P(yellow) = 3/10.

items.q: You roll a fair number cube with faces 1 to 6. What is P(a 4)?
items.e: 1 of the 6 faces works, so the probability is 1/6.

items.q: You roll a fair number cube with faces 1 to 6. What is P(an even number)?
items.e: 3 of the 6 faces work, so the probability is 3/6 = 1/2.

items.q: You roll a fair number cube with faces 1 to 6. What is P(a number greater than 4)?
items.e: 2 of the 6 faces work, so the probability is 2/6 = 1/3.

items.q: You roll a fair number cube with faces 1 to 6. What is P(a number less than 3)?
items.e: 2 of the 6 faces work, so the probability is 2/6 = 1/3.

items.q: You roll a fair number cube with faces 1 to 6. What is P(a multiple of 3)?
items.e: 2 of the 6 faces work, so the probability is 2/6 = 1/3.

items.q: You roll a fair number cube with faces 1 to 6. What is P(a prime number (2, 3 or 5))?
items.e: 3 of the 6 faces work, so the probability is 3/6 = 1/2.

items.q: Each letter of the word MISSISSIPPI is on its own card. You pick one card. What is P(S)?
items.e: There are 11 letters and 4 of them are S. P(S) = 4/11.

items.q: A class has 12 girls and 15 boys. The teacher picks one student at random. What is P(girl)?
items.e: 12 girls out of 27 students: 12/27 = 4/9. Not 4/5 (12/15): divide by all 27 students.

items.q: A month has 30 days. One day is picked at random. What is the probability that it is the 15th?
items.e: Only 1 of the 30 days works: 1/30.

items.q: A jar has 10 cards numbered 1 to 10. What is P(a number greater than 7)?
items.e: 8, 9 and 10 work: 3 out of 10 = 3/10.

items.q: The probability that it rains tomorrow is 14. What is the probability that it does not rain?
items.e: An event and its complement add to 1: 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.

items.q: The probability that it rains tomorrow is 27. What is the probability that it does not rain?
items.e: An event and its complement add to 1: 1 − 2/7 = 5/7.

items.q: The probability that it rains tomorrow is 58. What is the probability that it does not rain?
items.e: An event and its complement add to 1: 1 − 5/8 = 3/8.

items.q: The probability that it rains tomorrow is 310. What is the probability that it does not rain?
items.e: An event and its complement add to 1: 1 − 3/10 = 7/10.

items.q: The probability that it rains tomorrow is 16. What is the probability that it does not rain?
items.e: An event and its complement add to 1: 1 − 1/6 = 5/6.

items.q: The probability that it rains tomorrow is 712. What is the probability that it does not rain?
items.e: An event and its complement add to 1: 1 − 7/12 = 5/12.

items.q: P(win) = 0.35. What is P(not win)?
P(win) = 0.9. What is P(not win)?
P(win) = 0.02. What is P(not win)?
P(win) = 0.48. What is P(not win)?
P(win) = 0.7. What is P(not win)?
There is a 30% chance of snow. What is the chance of no snow?
There is an 85% chance of snow. What is the chance of no snow?
There is a 12% chance of snow. What is the chance of no snow?
A bag has 3 red, 4 blue and 5 green marbles. What is P(not green)?
items.e: 7 of the 12 marbles are not green (3 red + 4 blue). Or 1 − 5/12 = 7/12.

items.q: A spinner has 8 equal sections, 3 of them yellow. What is P(not yellow)?
items.e: 5 of the 8 sections are not yellow: 5/8. Check: 3/8 + 5/8 = 1.

items.q: You roll a number cube. What is P(not 6)?
items.e: 5 of the 6 faces are not 6: 5/6.

items.q: P(A) = 0.4. Which statement is true?
items.e: P(A) + P(not A) = 1, so P(not A) = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6.

items.q: A weather app says the chance of rain is 0%. What does that mean?
c: It is not expected to rain at all.
Rain and no rain are equally likely.
items.e: A probability of 0 means the event is impossible (or not expected).

items.q: A bag has only red and blue tiles. P(red) = 3/8. What is P(blue)?
items.e: There are only two colours, so P(blue) = 1 − 3/8 = 5/8.

items.q: A coin was flipped 50 times and landed on heads 28 times. What is the experimental probability of heads?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ total tries = 28/50 = 14/25.

items.q: A number cube was rolled 60 times. It showed 3 twelve times. What is the experimental probability of rolling a 3?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ total tries = 12/60 = 1/5.

items.q: A spinner was spun 40 times and landed on blue 14 times. What is the experimental probability of blue?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ total tries = 14/40 = 7/20.

items.q: A basketball player made 18 of 25 shots. What is the experimental probability of making a shot?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ total tries = 18/25 = 18/25.

items.q: Out of 80 cars that passed, 32 were white. What is the experimental probability of a white car?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ total tries = 32/80 = 2/5.

items.q: The probability of rolling a 5 is 1/6. You roll a number cube 120 times. About how many times should you expect a 5?
items.e: Multiply the probability by the number of tries. 1/6 × 120 = 20.

items.q: A spinner lands on red with probability 1/4. It is spun 200 times. About how many times will it land on red?
items.e: Multiply the probability by the number of tries. 1/4 × 200 = 50.

items.q: A player makes 70% of free throws. About how many will she make in 40 tries?
items.e: Multiply the probability by the number of tries. 0.7 × 40 = 28.

items.q: The probability a light bulb is broken is 0.02. About how many broken bulbs are in a box of 500?
items.e: Multiply the probability by the number of tries. 0.02 × 500 = 10.

items.q: A coin is flipped 300 times. About how many heads do you expect?
items.e: Multiply the probability by the number of tries. 1/2 × 300 = 150.

items.q: Out of 50 students surveyed, 15 walk to school. A school has 600 students. About how many walk to school?
items.e: Multiply the probability by the number of tries. 15/50 = 0.3, and 0.3 × 600 = 180.

items.q: A coin is flipped 10 times and lands on heads 7 times. What does this show?
c: The theoretical probability of heads is 7/10.
Experimental results can differ from the theoretical probability of 1/2.
The next flip will be tails.
items.e: With only 10 flips, results vary a lot. With many more flips, the fraction of heads usually gets closer to 1/2.

items.q: Which is most likely to give an experimental probability close to the theoretical probability?
items.e: More trials usually bring the experimental probability closer to the theoretical probability.

items.q: A spinner was spun 100 times: red 48, blue 27, green 25. Which spinner is most likely?
c: Red covers about half; blue and green about a quarter each.
items.e: 48/100 is close to 1/2, and 27/100 and 25/100 are close to 1/4.

items.q: A spinner landed on yellow 9 times in 30 spins. Based on this, what is the probability of yellow?
items.e: 9/30 = 3/10. Not 9/21: divide by all 30 spins.

items.q: A bag has 2 red and 8 blue marbles. You pick and replace a marble 50 times. About how many reds should you expect?
Theoretical P(green) = 1/3. In 60 spins, green came up 26 times. Which is true?
c: Green came up exactly as expected.
Green came up less than expected.
Green came up more than expected (20).
items.e: Expected: 1/3 × 60 = 20. 26 is more than 20.

items.q: A survey found that 12 of 40 people like jazz best. What is the experimental probability that a person likes jazz best?
Two number cubes are rolled 36 times. A sum of 7 came up 8 times. The theoretical probability is 6/36. Which is true?
c: The experimental probability (8/36) is a little higher than 6/36.
items.e: 8/36 is a little more than 6/36. Small differences are normal in experiments.

items.q: A spinner has 4 equal sections, 1 of them green. Ana spins it 80 times. About how many times should it land on green?
A raffle sells 250 tickets. You buy 5. What is the probability that you win?
items.e: 5 winning chances out of 250 tickets: 5/250 = 1/50.

items.q: A box has 6 chocolate, 4 vanilla and 10 strawberry cookies. You pick one. What is P(chocolate or vanilla)?
A class of 30 has 18 students with a pet. One is picked at random. What is P(no pet)?
A game: you win if a number cube shows 1 or 2. Your friend wins on 3, 4, 5 or 6. Is it fair?
c: No, your friend is twice as likely to win.
No, you are more likely to win.
Yes, it is a number cube.
items.e: P(you) = 2/6 = 1/3 and P(friend) = 4/6 = 2/3. A fair game needs equal chances.

items.q: A bag has 4 red marbles and some blue marbles. P(red) = 1/3. How many blue marbles are there?
items.e: If 4 is 1/3 of the total, the total is 12. 12 − 4 = 8 blue. Not 12: that is the total.

items.q: A spinner has 5 equal parts: 2 red and 3 blue. You spin 75 times. About how many times will it land on blue?
A drawer has 5 black socks and 7 white socks. You pick one in the dark. What is P(white)?
items.e: 7 white out of 12 socks: 7/12.

items.q: A store says 1 in every 40 cereal boxes has a prize. About how many prizes are in 1,000 boxes?
A quality check finds 3 bad phones in a sample of 150. The factory makes 5,000 phones. About how many are bad?
The letters of MATH are on 4 cards. You pick one. What is P(a vowel)?
items.e: Only A is a vowel: 1 out of 4.

items.q: A playlist has 20 songs: 8 pop, 7 rock and 5 jazz. It plays one at random. What is P(rock)?
items.e: 7 rock songs out of 20: 7/20. Not 7/13: divide by all 20 songs.

items.q: A meteorologist says there is a 60% chance of rain on each of the next 10 days. About how many rainy days should you expect?
items.e: 60% of 10 = 6 days.

items.q: A number from 1 to 20 is picked at random. What is P(a multiple of 4)?
Event A has probability 0.25 and event B has probability 0.6. Which is true?
c: B is more likely than A.
A is more likely than B.
items.e: 0.6 is greater than 0.25, so B is more likely.

items.q: A bag has 3 red, 3 blue and 3 green cubes. You take out one blue cube and keep it. Then you pick one more. What is P(blue)?
items.e: Now there are 8 cubes and 2 are blue: 2/8 = 1/4.

items.q: A spinner is spun 120 times and lands on purple 30 times. The spinner has 8 equal sections. How many sections are probably purple?
items.e: 30/120 = 1/4 of the spins. 1/4 of 8 sections is 2.

items.q: Two coins are flipped. The outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT. What is P(exactly one head)?
items.e: HT and TH have exactly one head: 2 out of 4 = 1/2. Not 1/3: HT and TH are different outcomes.

items.q: A school has 400 students. 140 are in Grade 7. A student is chosen at random. What is P(Grade 7)?
Which spinner gives P(red) = 3/8?
items.e: 3 red out of 8 equal sections is 3/8. 3 red and 8 not red would be 3/11.

items.q: A survey of 60 students finds 24 prefer soccer. In a school of 450, about how many prefer soccer?
